meta.title_en: Dyslipidaemia: LDL Biology, Statins, Ezetimibe, PCSK9 Inhibitors and Risk Targets

content.intro: Dyslipidaemia is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, affecting millions of people worldwide. The pathophysiology of dyslipidaemia involves an imbalance in lipid metabolism, leading to elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. LDL cholesterol is a key contributor to the development of atherosclerosis, a condition characterized by the buildup of plaque in the arterial walls. The epidemiology of dyslipidaemia is complex, with multiple factors contributing to its development, including genetics, diet, and lifestyle. According to the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines (2021), dyslipidaemia is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

sections.heading: LDL Biology and Atherosclerosis
sections.text: LDL cholesterol plays a central role in the development of atherosclerosis. Elevated levels of LDL cholesterol lead to the formation of foam cells, which are lipid-laden macrophages that contribute to the growth of atherosclerotic plaques. The ESC guidelines (2021) recommend targeting LDL cholesterol levels to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. Statins, such as atorvastatin (40-80 mg/day) and rosuvastatin (10-20 mg/day), are effective in reducing LDL cholesterol levels and have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in numerous landmark trials, including the ASTEROID trial (2006) and the IMPROVE-IT trial (2015).

sections.heading: Genetic Factors and Dyslipidaemia
sections.text: Genetic factors play a significant role in the development of dyslipidaemia. Certain genetic mutations, such as those affecting the LDL receptor, can lead to elevated levels of LDL cholesterol. The AHA guidelines (2019) recommend genetic testing for individuals with a family history of dyslipidaemia. Ezetimibe (10 mg/day) is a useful adjunct to statin therapy in individuals with genetic dyslipidaemia, as it has been shown to reduce LDL cholesterol levels by inhibiting the intestinal absorption of cholesterol.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Factors and Dyslipidaemia
sections.text: Lifestyle factors, such as diet and physical activity, also contribute to the development of dyslipidaemia. The NICE guidelines (2019) recommend a healthy diet and regular physical activity to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. A diet low in saturated fats and high in fruits and vegetables can help to reduce LDL cholesterol levels. Regular physical activity, such as walking or jogging, can also help to improve lipid profiles and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

content.clinical_pearl: The use of statins has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events by 25-30% in individuals with elevated LDL cholesterol levels (Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration, 2010).

content.intro: Dyslipidaemia can present with a range of symptoms, from asymptomatic to severe cardiovascular disease. The clinical presentation of dyslipidaemia depends on the severity of the lipid abnormality and the presence of other cardiovascular risk factors. According to the AHA guidelines (2019), individuals with dyslipidaemia should be evaluated for other cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

sections.heading: Asymptomatic Dyslipidaemia
sections.text: Many individuals with dyslipidaemia are asymptomatic, and the condition is often detected during routine lipid screening. The ESC guidelines (2021) recommend routine lipid screening for all adults aged 40-75 years. Asymptomatic dyslipidaemia can be managed with lifestyle modifications, such as diet and exercise, and pharmacotherapy, such as statins.

sections.heading: Symptomatic Dyslipidaemia
sections.text: Symptomatic dyslipidaemia can present with a range of symptoms, including chest pain, shortness of breath, and fatigue. The AHA guidelines (2019) recommend that individuals with symptomatic dyslipidaemia be evaluated for coronary artery disease and other cardiovascular conditions. PCSK9 inhibitors, such as alirocumab (75-150 mg every 2 weeks) and evolocumab (140 mg every 2 weeks), are effective in reducing LDL cholesterol levels in individuals with symptomatic dyslipidaemia.

sections.heading: Dyslipidaemia in Special Populations
sections.text: Dyslipidaemia can occur in special populations, such as children and pregnant women. The NICE guidelines (2019) recommend that children with a family history of dyslipidaemia be screened for lipid abnormalities. Pregnant women with dyslipidaemia should be managed with lifestyle modifications and pharmacotherapy, as needed, to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

content.clinical_pearl: The use of PCSK9 inhibitors has been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events by 15-20% in individuals with symptomatic dyslipidaemia (ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial, 2018).

content.intro: The diagnosis of dyslipidaemia involves a range of investigations, including lipid profiling and cardiovascular risk assessment. According to the ESC guidelines (2021), lipid profiling should include measurement of total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and triglycerides.

sections.heading: Lipid Profiling
sections.text: Lipid profiling is a critical component of the diagnosis of dyslipidaemia. The AHA guidelines (2019) recommend that lipid profiles be measured in all adults aged 20-75 years. Lipid profiling can be used to diagnose dyslipidaemia and to monitor the effectiveness of treatment. The NICE guidelines (2019) recommend that lipid profiles be measured at least annually in individuals with dyslipidaemia.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular Risk Assessment
sections.text: Cardiovascular risk assessment is an important component of the diagnosis of dyslipidaemia. The ESC guidelines (2021) recommend that cardiovascular risk be assessed using a risk calculator, such as the Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation (SCORE) system. Cardiovascular risk assessment can be used to identify individuals at high risk of cardiovascular disease and to guide treatment decisions.

sections.heading: Genetic Testing
sections.text: Genetic testing can be used to diagnose genetic dyslipidaemia. The AHA guidelines (2019) recommend that genetic testing be considered in individuals with a family history of dyslipidaemia. Genetic testing can be used to identify genetic mutations that affect lipid metabolism and to guide treatment decisions.

content.intro: The treatment and management of dyslipidaemia involve a range of strategies, including lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy, and cardiovascular risk reduction. According to the AHA guidelines (2019), the primary goal of treatment is to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

sections.heading: Lifestyle Modifications
sections.text: Lifestyle modifications are an important component of the treatment and management of dyslipidaemia. The ESC guidelines (2021) recommend a healthy diet, regular physical activity, and weight management to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. Lifestyle modifications can be used to reduce LDL cholesterol levels and to improve overall cardiovascular health.

sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy
sections.text: Pharmacotherapy is a critical component of the treatment and management of dyslipidaemia. The AHA guidelines (2019) recommend the use of statins, such as atorvastatin (40-80 mg/day) and rosuvastatin (10-20 mg/day), to reduce LDL cholesterol levels. PCSK9 inhibitors, such as alirocumab (75-150 mg every 2 weeks) and evolocumab (140 mg every 2 weeks), can be used in individuals who are intolerant of statins or who require additional LDL cholesterol reduction.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction
sections.text: Cardiovascular risk reduction is an important component of the treatment and management of dyslipidaemia. The ESC guidelines (2021) recommend that individuals with dyslipidaemia be evaluated for other cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Cardiovascular risk reduction can be achieved through lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy, and other interventions, such as aspirin therapy and blood pressure management.
